description:
Ley de Conservación del Mate | San Luis, Argentina 🇦🇷

"El mate no se crea ni se destruye, solo pasa de mano en mano mientras exploramos el cosmos."

Somos un equipo apasionado por la ciencia, la tecnología y la exploración espacial participando en el NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 desde San Luis, Argentina.

Nuestro Desafío: Planet X and SPHEREx
La misión SPHEREx de la NASA mapea todo el cielo cada seis meses en 102 bandas de luz infrarroja cercana, capturando más de mil millones de objetos celestes. Nuestro objetivo es desarrollar una plataforma web interactiva, intuitiva y abierta al público que permita comparar imágenes astronómicas a lo largo del tiempo para que cualquier persona o científico ciudadano pueda descubrir objetos en movimiento: asteroides, cometas, enanas marrones e incluso el esquivo Planeta X.

¿A quiénes buscamos?
Estamos abiertos a sumar integrantes con ganas de aprender, crear y cebar buenos mates:

Programadores / Desarrolladores Web (Frontend & Backend): React, Next.js, TypeScript, Python, WebGL/Canvas o manejo de APIs y datos astronómicos.

Diseñadores UI/UX y Gráficos: Para diseñar una interfaz visual atractiva, clara e intuitiva para explorar el cielo y presentar datos complejos de forma simple.

Ciencia de Datos / Astronomía / Física: Procesamiento de imágenes, alineación temporal y detección de anomalías o movimiento.

Comunicación, Storytelling y Video Pitch: Redacción, edición de video y armado de la presentación final del proyecto.

Contacto directo:

summary: AstroExplore is an open-source astrophysics and citizen-science web platform designed to inspect calibrated observations from NASA's SPHEREx mission across all 102 near-infrared spectral channels (0.75 to 5.00 µm). Connecting directly to NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA) Simple Image Access (SIA v2) and Image Server (IBE) APIs, the platform decodes seven-extension FITS files client-side in TypeScript without requiring specialized desktop astronomy software. Users can animate multi-epoch sky exposures in a digital blink comparator, compute variance-normalized differential images (B - A) with Z-score hypothesis testing to distinguish moving planetary candidates and ultra-cool brown dwarfs from stationary variable stars, and co-add the 17 channels per detector array to boost the signal-to-noise ratio by a factor of 4.123 (+312.3%). Furthermore, the system extracts on-the-fly 102-band spectral energy distributions, evaluates Beer-Lambert optical depths across eight molecular absorption features (H2O, CH4, NH3, CO2, CO, PAHs), derives Wien and Stefan-Boltzmann radiative thermodynamics, performs least-squares astrometric trajectory fitting, and provides a dual-mode interface for both researchers and students.
details:
1. Executive Overview & Official Project Repositories

Team: Ley de Conservación del Mate — Faculty of Physical, Mathematical and Natural Sciences, National University of San Luis (UNSL), San Luis, Argentina (Jonás Villegas, Tomás Achával, Joaquin Barrionuevo, Facundo Bazán, Uriel Domínguez, and Jeremías Nolte).
Challenge: Planet X and SPHEREx (2026 NASA International Space Apps Challenge).

  • Primary Source Code Repository (GitHub): https://github.com/jonasvillegass/NASA---SAC---2026
  • Master Project Archive, Technical Dossier & Obsidian Knowledge Graph (Google Drive Mother Folder): https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1TIUwAkfaNALHzs7UsjKtbPUVdvedDxpk?usp=sharin
  • Page: https://astroexplore.vercel.app/

Since 2025, NASA's SPHEREx (Spectro-Photometer for the History of the Universe, Epoch of Reionization and Ices Explorer) mission has surveyed the entire celestial sphere every six months across 102 continuous near-infrared spectral bands (0.75 to 5.00 μm), recording spectrophotometry for over one billion celestial sources. Moving solar system objects (trans-Neptunian objects, hypothetical Planet X / Planet Nine candidates, asteroids, and comets), high-proper-motion sub-stellar bodies (ultra-cool T and Y brown dwarfs), and variable stars reveal themselves by shifting position or flux across semi-annual epochs separated by a 2 AU orbital baseline. However, raw multi-extension FITS products hosted at the NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA) remain inaccessible to the general public and computationally cumbersome for rapid browser-based reconnaissance.

AstroExplore bridges this gap by transforming calibrated SPHEREx Data Release 1 (spherex_dr1, spherex_dr1_deep) and Quick Release (spherex_qr3) archives into an interactive, zero-installation web laboratory that executes rigorous astrometric, statistical, thermodynamic, and astrochemical reductions directly in the user's browser.

2. System Architecture & Live NASA/IPAC IRSA Archival Pipeline

  1. Direct IVOA Simple Image Access (SIA v2) & IBE Cutout Pipeline: Queries the official NASA/IPAC IRSA SIA v2 endpoint (https://irsa.ipac.caltech.edu/SIA) by ICRS J2000 right ascension and declination (supporting both decimal degrees and sexagesimal HMS/DMS notation, plus live object resolution via CDS Sesame / SIMBAD / NED) and streams calibrated angular FITS cutouts via the IRSA Image Server (https://irsa.ipac.caltech.edu/ibe/data/spherex/).
    • HDU[0] PRIMARY: Mission telemetry, observation timestamps (MJD-OBS), detector array identifier (D1–D6), and gnomonic (TAN) World Coordinate System (WCS) projection matrices (6.2 arcsec/pixel plate scale).
    • HDU[1] IMAGE: Calibrated surface brightness matrices in megajanskys per steradian (MJy/sr).
    • HDU[2] FLAGS: 32-bit per-pixel quality bitmask; our pipeline applies bitmask filtering (0x0037 / 0x7ffffffe) to mask cosmic-ray hits, detector saturation, overflow, and dead pixels prior to statistical analysis.
    • HDU[3] VARIANCE: Per-pixel noise variance (σ2) used for minimum-variance weighting and Z-score significance maps.
    • HDU[4] ZODI: Empirical solar system zodiacal dust foreground model, subtracted in real time (I_clean = IMAGE - ZODI) to isolate faint sub-stellar and extragalactic emission.
    • HDU[5] EPSF: Effective Point Spread Function kernel for morphological profile validation.
    • HDU[6] WCS-WAVE: Two-dimensional Linear Variable Filter (LVF) dispersion lookup table mapping pixel coordinates (x, y) to exact central wavelength λ (μm) and bandwidth Δλ.
  2. Scientific Integrity & Zero-Mock-Data Guarantee: In strict adherence to observational standards, the application contains zero hardcoded or synthetic flux arrays. Every pixel, epoch timestamp, variance estimate, and spectral point is computed dynamically from live NASA/IPAC IRSA responses, with automated API health diagnostics (src/lib/apiError.ts).

3. Formal Physical, Statistical & Chemical Formulation (Six Quantitative Outputs)

All analytical engines are grounded in university-level engineering and physics textbooks from the National University of San Luis (UNSL) curriculum:

  • Output 1 — Minimum-Variance Detector Array Co-Addition (SNR × √17 ≈ 4.123, +312.3% Gain): Grounded in the Central Limit Theorem and Minimum-Variance Unbiased Estimation (Devore, 2016), stacking the N = 17 spectral channels within each HgCdTe detector array (D1–D6) using inverse-variance weights w_i(x,y) = 1 / σ_i^2(x,y) yields the optimal estimator I_coadd(x,y) = [Σ w_i I_i(x,y)] / [Σ w_i]. For uncorrelated instrumental noise, the combined Signal-to-Noise Ratio increases as SNR_coadd = √(Σ SNR_i^2) ≈ √17 · SNR_band ≈ 4.123 × SNR_band (+312.3%), enabling detection of ultra-faint brown dwarfs and trans-Neptunian candidates invisible in individual narrow-band exposures.
  • Output 2 — Multi-Epoch Differential Photometry (B − A) & Z-Score Hypothesis Testing: Given two calibrated exposures I_1(x,y) and I_2(x,y) separated by Δt ≈ 6 months, the engine computes the variance-normalized residual statistic Z(x,y) = [I_2(x,y) - I_1(x,y)] / √[σ_1^2(x,y) + σ_2^2(x,y)] (Kreyszig, 2014; Devore, 2016). Stationary background stars cancel to Z ≈ 0. Pixels exceeding |Z| ≥ 3.0σ (two-tailed p = 0.0027) and |Z| ≥ 5.0σ (p = 5.73 × 10−7) are automatically classified into moving dipoles (paired negative/positive lobes diagnostic of proper motion or orbital translation) versus stationary variable monopoles (concentric flux modulation at fixed celestial coordinates).
  • Output 3 — Spherical Astrometry, Multi-Epoch Least-Squares Trajectory Fitting & Proper Motion Vectors: Using gnomonic WCS transformations with spherical cosine correction Δα* = Δα cos(δ) and prime-meridian continuity across α = 0° / 360°, our trajectory engine (src/lib/trajectory.ts) performs Ordinary Least-Squares (OLS) linear regression across multi-epoch centroids to derive proper motion components (μ_α*, μ_δ), total angular speed μ_total = √[(μ_α*)^2 + (μ_δ)^2] [arcsec/yr], and position angle θ = atan2(μ_α*, μ_δ) (Young & Freedman, 2018; Stewart, 2018).
  • Output 4 — Trigonometric Parallax, Keplerian Kinematics & Escape Velocity Constraints: Exploiting SPHEREx's 2 AU semi-annual orbital baseline, the astrometric engine relates annual parallax p [arcsec] to heliocentric distance d_pc = 1 / p (d_ly = 3.2616 · d_pc), transverse linear velocity v_t = 4.74 · μ_total · d_pc [km/s], and gravitational escape velocity v_esc = √(2GM / R) to evaluate volatile retention on outer solar system bodies (Serway & Jewett, 2008).
  • Output 5 — Radiative Thermodynamics (Planck, Wien & Stefan-Boltzmann Laws): From 3×3 target-centered aperture photometry across 0.75–5.00 μm, the spectral engine identifies peak emission wavelength λ_peak to compute effective blackbody temperature via Wien's displacement law T_eff = 2897.77 μm·K / λ_peak, bolometric surface radiant emittance via the Stefan-Boltzmann law j* = σ T_eff^4 (σ = 5.670 × 10^-8 W·m^-2·K^-4), and inter-array infrared color indices Color_(D6-D1) = -2.5 log10(F_D6 / F_D1), distinguishing cold 250 K sub-stellar objects (such as WISE 0855) from main-sequence field stars (Çengel & Boles, 2012; Halliday, Resnick, & Krane, 2001; Zill, 2011).
  • Output 6 — 102-Band Infrared Astrochemistry, Beer-Lambert Optical Depth & CHNOPS Habitability Assessment: Across the six LVF detector arrays (D1–D3 at R = 41, D4 at R = 35, D5 at R = 110, D6 at R = 130), the chemical engine (src/lib/spectralAnalysis.ts) computes optical depth τ(λ) = ln[F_cont(λ) / F_obs(λ)] and relative absorption percentage D_abs(%) = [1 - F_obs / F_cont] × 100% via the Beer-Lambert law (Chang & Goldsby, 2013) across eight diagnostic molecular vibration-rotation bands: H2O vapor (1.40 μm, D2), CH4 (1.66, 2.20, and 3.32 μm, D3/D4), NH3 (2.95 μm, D4), H2O ice (3.05 μm, D4), PAHs (3.29 μm, D4), CO2 (4.27 μm, D5), and CO (4.67 μm, D6). An integrated Region-of-Interest (ROI) classifier computes probability distributions across six astrophysical archetypes and evaluates a weighted five-factor habitability and prebiotic CHNOPS score (Water 30%, Organic Carbon 25%, Biogenic Nitrogen 20%, Wien Thermal Regime 15%, Radiative Stability 10%).

4. Interactive Discovery Workflow & User Experience

  • Split-Screen Dual-Map Workspace (ViewerPanel.tsx): Map 1 integrates CDS Aladin Lite v3 with multi-mission sky surveys (2MASS, AllWISE, Gaia DR3) and interactive grid selection; Map 2 provides a full-screen multi-tab laboratory supporting individual FITS inspection, D1–D6 detector mosaics, on-the-fly SED spectrograms, the multi-epoch Blink comparator, and an interactive Detector Guide.
  • Astronomical Stretch & Colormap Pipeline: Real-time HTML5 Canvas 2D pixel processing with four transfer functions (linear, sqrt, log, asinh) and six scientific colormaps (viridis, inferno, magma, plasma, cividis, grayscale).
  • Interactive Region-of-Interest (ROI) Modal (RoiAnalysisModal.tsx): Users can draw rectangular ROIs directly over any celestial source to trigger automated multi-epoch trajectory regression, 102-band spectral extraction, celestial archetype classification, and CHNOPS astrobiological scoring, plus launch in-place target searches via NewSearchModal.tsx.
  • Dual Reading Modes, Acoustic Feedback & Reproducible Deep-Linking: Toggles between Explorer Mode (plain-language explanations for students and citizen scientists) and Scientific Mode (variance telemetry and formal equations for researchers), enhanced by a Web Audio API velocity-reactive cursor synthesizer (cursorAudio.ts), full bilingual support (EN/ES), and deterministic URL state permalinks (?ra=...&dec=...&fov=...).

5. Benchmark Validation Catalog

  1. WISE J085510.83-071442.5 (RA = 133.795°, Dec = -7.245°): Coldest known Y4 sub-stellar brown dwarf (Teff ≈ 250 K, distance 2.28 pc, μ ≈ 8.1 arcsec/yr), validating thermal detection in bands D5–D6 (4.0–5.0 μm) as a direct analog for Planet X.
  2. Barnard's Star (RA = 269.452°, Dec = +4.693°): Highest proper-motion star in the sky (μ = 10.3 arcsec/yr ≈ 1.66 SPHEREx pixels/yr), validating multi-epoch dipole detection and least-squares trajectory fitting.
  3. Epsilon Indi Ba/Bb (RA = 331.068°, Dec = -56.786°): Binary T1 + T6 brown dwarf system (μ = 4.7 arcsec/yr), validating deep CH4 and H2O absorption band recovery in arrays D2–D4.
  4. RW Aurigae (RA = 76.956°, Dec = +30.401°): T Tauri variable star with an active protoplanetary disk, validating stationary monopole variability and infrared dust excess.
  5. R Draconis (RA = 248.172°, Dec = +66.754°): Mira-type pulsating Asymptotic Giant Branch (AGB) variable star, validating large-amplitude temporal flux modulation.

6. Academic Literature & Engineering References (APA 7th Edition)

  • Çengel, Y. A., & Boles, M. A. (2012). Thermodynamics: An engineering approach (7th ed.). McGraw-Hill. (Chapter 12 & Chapter 18: Planck blackbody distribution, Wien's displacement law, and Stefan-Boltzmann radiative emittance).
  • Chang, R., & Goldsby, K. A. (2013). Chemistry (11th ed.). McGraw-Hill. (Chapters 7, 9, & 11: Quantum vibrational spectroscopy, Beer-Lambert optical depth, and interstellar molecular ices H2O, CH4, NH3, CO2, and CO).
  • Crill, B. P., Werner, M., Akeson, R., Ashby, M., Bleem, L., Bock, J. J., Bryan, S., Burnham, J., Byun, J., Chang, T.-C., Chiang, Y.-K., Condon, S., Cooray, A., Doré, O., Dowell, C. D., Dubois-Aronin, L., Eimer, J., Faisst, A., Filippazzo, J., ... Zemcov, M. (2020). SPHEREx: NASA's near-infrared spectrophotometric all-sky survey. Proceedings of the SPIE, 11443, 114430I. https://doi.org/10.1117/12.2567224
  • Devore, J. L. (2016). Probability and statistics for engineering and the sciences (9th ed.). Cengage Learning. (Chapters 5, 7, & 8: Central Limit Theorem, Minimum-Variance Unbiased Estimation for 17-channel detector co-addition, and two-sample Z-score hypothesis testing).
  • Doré, O., Bock, J., Ashby, M., Capak, P., Cooray, A., de Putter, R., Eifler, T., Flagey, N., Gong, Y., Habib, S., Heitmann, K., Hirata, C., Jeong, W.-S., Katti, R., Korngut, P., Krause, E., Lee, D.-H., Lisse, C., Masters, D., ... Zemcov, M. (2014). Cosmology with the SPHEREx all-sky spectral survey. arXiv Astrophysics. https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.1412.4872
  • Halliday, D., Resnick, R., & Krane, K. S. (2001). Physics (Vol. 2, 4th ed.). John Wiley & Sons. (Chapters 41 & 42: Poynting flux and surface brightness conversion from MJy/sr).
  • Kreyszig, E. (2014). Advanced engineering mathematics (10th ed.). John Wiley & Sons. (Chapters 7, 11, & 12: Affine WCS matrix transformations, 2D Fourier spatial filtering, and PSF convolution).
  • Piskunov, N. (1977). Differential and integral calculus (Vols. 1–2). Mir Publishers. (Chapter 13: Differential equations of orbital trajectories across semi-annual baselines).
  • Serway, R. A., & Jewett, J. W. (2008). Physics for scientists and engineers with modern physics (7th ed.). Cengage Learning. (Chapters 13 & 14: Universal gravitation, planetary escape velocity, and hydrostatic atmospheric retention).
  • Stewart, J. (2018). Calculus: Early transcendentals (8th ed.). Cengage Learning. (Chapters 14 & 15: Directional brightness gradients for sub-pixel centroiding and double polar integrals for aperture photometry).
  • Young, H. D., & Freedman, R. A. (2018). Sears and Zemansky's university physics with modern physics (14th ed.). Pearson. (Chapters 3, 13, 32, 34, & 36: Relative velocity vectors, Keplerian orbital mechanics, Rayleigh diffraction limit, and trigonometric parallax).
  • Zill, D. G. (2011). Calculus: Early transcendentals (4th ed.). McGraw-Hill. (Chapter 9: Taylor series expansion for the Rayleigh-Jeans infrared limit).

7. Super Intelligence (SI / AI) Transparency Disclosure

In compliance with NASA Space Apps Challenge guidelines, our team discloses the use of Google Gemini (Antigravity IDE) and Anthropic Claude as software engineering, code debugging, mathematical verification, and English editorial assistants during the hackathon. All architectural decisions, physical models, textbook derivations, and experimental validations were conceived and directed by the human team members at the National University of San Luis. No artificial intelligence tool was used to generate synthetic astronomical imagery or fabricated measurements; 100% of FITS cutouts, coordinates, and spectrophotometric fluxes are retrieved live from NASA/IPAC IRSA.
